What does a gold assay actually tell you?

Explore what content, fineness and sample relevance mean in practical terms.

KNOWLEDGE & INSIGHTS

Ideas for interpreting the questions behind materials and laboratory reports.

← Back to insights

Explore what content, fineness and sample relevance mean in practical terms.

The question behind the measurement

Gold may appear as an ingot, jewellery, grains, dust or a component within mineral-bearing material. These forms differ in ways that influence sampling and interpretation. An assay begins by defining what is being measured and why the result is needed.

A weight on a scale tells you how much material is present, not the proportion that is gold. Appearance is similarly insufficient: alloying metals, surface coatings and heterogeneous particles can all affect what an item looks like without establishing its overall composition.

Understanding fineness

Fineness expresses the proportion of gold within the tested material. It may be described in parts per thousand, mass percent or another recognised convention. The units must be clear to avoid confusing concentration with total mass.

The laboratory method and specimen preparation matter. Surface observations may not establish the composition of the interior; a sub-sample of a mixed lot may not capture the variability of the whole. The result belongs to the specimen that was actually examined.

Using the result responsibly

A meaningful report connects an identifier to the measured material, records suitable method context and presents the finding in interpretable units. Comparing results between different testing approaches requires understanding their scope and limitations.

If a commercial decision concerns a large lot, a representative sampling strategy can be as important as the analytical method. Ask how the sample was selected before assuming that a single result describes all material in the shipment.
